reconcile.connective: Matthew Henry notes Mark's one beggar against Matthew's two, then reads Luke's 'near Jericho' as ambiguous enough to fit either approach or departure.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible presses both points as flat contradictions: entering versus leaving Jericho, and one beggar versus two.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/jericho.html and contra/blindmen.html

excerpts.excerpt_text: Mark gives us an account of one, and names him, whom he cured as he went out of Jericho, Mar 10:46. Matthew speaks of two whom he cured as they departed from Jericho, Mat 20:30. Luke says it was en tō engizein auton - when he was near to Jericho, which might be when he was going out of it as well as when he was coming into it.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: MHC juxtaposes Mark's single named beggar against Matthew's two, then directly argues the location tension away by reading Luke's Greek phrase for 'near Jericho' as ambiguous between approach and departure.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact triad (Matt 20:30, Mark 10:46, Luke 18:35, 38) under 'Historical Discrepancies,' pp. 386-387 (verified via archive.org djvu text of examinationofall00hale), canvassing three harmonizing options: three blind men healed (one entering, two leaving), two men healed with Matthew condensing both into the departure, or Luke's Greek verb read simply as 'nigh/near' without specifying direction -- with Mark and Luke naming only the better-known of the two beggars.

link.title: Did Jesus heal two blind men (Matthew 20:29-34) or one blind man (Mark 10:46-52; Luke 18:35-43)?
